summary: An excerpt from a fiction book (Book 11, part 6) in which a young girl explains how her family's children were named after relatives, books, and people, mentioning her mother's hopes and her father's bad luck. She then talks with Mr. Cobb about shoes, school, her plans to become a painter or teacher, and the difference between calling her home Randall's Farm versus Sunnybrook Farm. The excerpt ends with Mr. Cobb unable to evade a reply under Rebecca's piercing gaze.
one_line: Excerpt from a novel where Rebecca explains her family's naming customs and debates farm names with Mr. Cobb.
key_facts: Mira was named after aunt Miranda in Riverboro in hopes it might do some good, but it didn't, and she is now called Mira.
Hannah is named after Hannah at the Window Binding Shoes.
The narrator is named after a character taken out of Ivanhoe.
Mark is named after his uncle Marquis de Lafayette, who died a twin.
Jenny is named for a singer, and Fanny is named for a beautiful dancer.
Mother says Jenny and Fanny are misfits because Jenny can't carry a tune and Fanny is kind of stiff-legged.
Mother would like to call the children by their middle names but says it wouldn't be fair to father.
The narrator says her father had bad luck and everything was against him, and he would not have died otherwise.
The narrator's shoes are spandy new and have to last six months, and she cannot go barefoot in Riverboro without shaming aunt Mirandy.
The narrator plans to attend the seminary at Wareham in two years, which mother says ought to be the making of her.
The narrator wants to be a painter like Miss Ross, though mother thinks she had better teach.
The family's farm is called Randall's Farm by mother, but the narrator calls it Sunnybrook Farm.
Mr. Cobb remarks that it doesn't make a difference what you call a farm so long as you know where it is.
The narrator insists that names make a difference and asks Mr. Cobb what Sunnybrook Farm makes him think of.
Mr. Cobb is uneasy about replying, and Rebecca's eyes are described as searchlights piercing the fiction of his brain.
